extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and scholars studying peer review, peer review bias, or scientometrics
extracted.subtask_short: empirical analysis of peer review sentiment
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical text-analysis study comparing the sentiment and tone of peer reviews by 'Reviewer 2' versus other reviewers using measurable textual metrics from BMJ open peer reviews, with regression adjustment for manuscript-level fixed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count
rubrics_metrics.description: Tally the word count of each peer review (the average peer review was 612 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes that harsher peer reviews would be longer; used as one of five numeric outcomes. Adjusted mean word counts were compared between Reviewer 2 and other reviewers (e.g., adjusted 630 vs 606 words, P = .16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative phrases count
rubrics_metrics.description: Count occurrences of negative phrases in each review (manually classified from an automatically generated list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes more negative phrases indicate a harsher review; manual classification was performed in a blinded fashion (see Supplementary Table 1). Used as a numeric outcome in regression models (adjusted 8.7 vs 8.4, P = .29).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive phrases count
rubrics_metrics.description: Count occurrences of positive phrases in each review (manually classified from an automatically generated list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes fewer positive phrases indicate a harsher review; used as a numeric outcome in regression models (adjusted 4.2 vs 4.1, P = .10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question marks (interrogative tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the number of question marks in each review as a proxy for interrogative tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes harsher reviews would contain more questions; used as a numeric outcome (adjusted 4.8 vs 4.6, P = .26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the word 'please' (request frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count instances of the word 'please' to capture requests or directive language in reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes more requests (e.g., 'please' conduct an analysis) are indicative of harsher or more demanding reviews; used as a numeric outcome (adjusted 1.0 vs 1.0, P = .80).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of 'harsher' review
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'harsher' reviews as those that are longer, with more negative phrases, more questions and requests, and fewer positive phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hypothesis guided metric selection. The study tested this operationalization using the five numeric measures above rather than an overall subjective judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer role labeling (definition of Reviewer 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Reviewer 2 as the second reviewer to return comments in the BMJ decision letters, irrespective of the order reviewers were asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural definition is necessary for assigning reviews to Reviewer 2 versus other reviewers; it may not generalize to journals that do not track reviewer return order similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-manuscript comparison (manuscript-level fixed effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use manuscript-level fixed effects to compare reviews for the same manuscript (primary adjusted analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological standard controls for manuscript-level heterogeneity by effectively comparing Reviewer 2 to other reviewers for the same manuscript, reducing confounding from manuscript characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on initial (first-decision) reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict analysis to peer reviews from manuscripts' first decision because not all manuscripts had subsequent peer reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inclusion criterion standardizes which round of review is analyzed and avoids bias from unequal numbers of revision rounds across manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual classification of key phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Manually classify commonly used phrases as negative or positive based on a blinded assessment of an automatically generated list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledged as a limitation; alternative approaches include manually characterizing all reviews or training a machine-learning algorithm on a manually labeled subset to predict review sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate outcome modeling and use of linear regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a separate linear regression for each outcome (words, negative phrases, positive phrases, question marks, 'please') with a binary indicator for Reviewer 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unadjusted models compared means; adjusted models included manuscript fixed effects. Adjusted mean outcomes were calculated using marginal standardization (predictive margins). This statistical approach is the standard used to test differences between Reviewer 2 and other reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample inclusion criteria (journal and reviewer counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include open peer reviews of research manuscripts published in the BMJ from 2015–2020 that had 2 to 5 peer reviewers (n=2546 reviews of 794 manuscripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using BMJ's open review policy provides publicly available text but may limit generalizability; the study notes this limitation and cites literature on the (lack of) effect of open review on review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between recommendation outcomes and textual sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that prior work focused on reviewer recommendations (accept/reject) while this study focuses on textual sentiment of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different outcome definitions (recommendation vs text-based sentiment) require different measurement strategies and may yield different conclusions; researchers should choose outcomes aligned with their research question.
